subsection: 5. The design process and garment construction

notes.b: Making a garment well starts long before the first cut. The design process is a fixed sequence of seven stages that takes you from the brief (the task you are set) to a finished garment that has been judged against that brief.
points: 1. Define and analyse the brief: identify who the garment is for, its purpose, the occasion, the budget and any constraints, so you know exactly what the garment must achieve.
2. Investigate and research: gather ideas from magazines, fabric samples, pattern books and observation of current trends, so your design is informed rather than guessed.
3. Generate possible ideas: sketch several designs, varying line, shape, colour and pattern, so you have real choices to compare.
4. Present the ideas: a labelled fashion sketch and a short written description show the chosen design features and why that design was chosen.
5. Refine the design: adjust the chosen design, the fabric and the trimmings (the decorative extras) until they meet the brief.
6. Implement: plan the work, select fabric and pattern, cut, construct and finish the garment.
7. Evaluate: assess the finished garment against the brief for fit, finish, comfort, function and appearance, and note improvements for next time.

The design specification is a list of what the garment must be and do: the wearer, its use, fabric needs, size and fit, care, cost, time and key features. It turns the brief into a checklist you can design and evaluate against.
notes.tip: When asked to outline the design process, give all seven steps in order with a few words on each. Do not jump from research straight to construction, a common way to lose marks.

notes.b: A design has to be communicated before it is made. A fashion sketch shows what the garment will look like, and a written description spells out the details a sketch cannot.
points: A fashion sketch shows the garment's line (the direction of its seams and edges), shape, proportion (how the parts relate in size) and harmony, and it can show colour and fabric.
The front view and, where needed, the back view show the design features, and the sketch must label them so the maker can see what is intended.
The written description covers colour, design, line, proportion, shape, pockets, seams, neckline, sleeves, fabric and finishes, and accessories.
Each design feature named in the description must be visible in the sketch, so the two match and nothing in the description is left unexplained.
Diagram: a labelled front-view fashion sketch, with the features (neckline, sleeves, pockets, seams, fabric) labelled.
notes.tip: For a sketch-and-describe question, draw a front view, label the features and name the fabric. Make sure everything you describe can be seen in the sketch.

notes.b: The fabric decides how a garment looks, hangs and wears, so it must suit both the purpose and the design. Fabric tests help you decide, and the notions (the small items used to make up a garment) must suit the fabric too.
points: Fabric is chosen for its suitability to the purpose: its absorbency, shrinkage, water repellence and crease recovery. Tests on these properties inform the choice.
A fabric test sample is washed and dried to check shrinkage before cutting, so the finished garment still fits after laundering.

Fabric choice must match the design: a soft drape suits a flowing skirt, while a crisp fabric holds the shape of a tailored jacket. Stretch suits fitted or sportswear, and easy-care fabric suits everyday wear.
The fabric must also fit the wearer's budget.
Notions such as zips, buttons, interfacing, lining, thread, elastic and trims should be chosen to match the fabric's weight, care needs and colour.
Interfacing (a layer sewn or fused inside to stiffen the fabric) gives body and support at collars, cuffs, waistbands and buttonholes, so these areas keep their shape.

notes.h: Selecting and reading a commercial pattern
notes.b: A commercial pattern is a full-scale tissue paper pattern sold in a sealed envelope. Choosing the right one, and reading what is on the envelope, saves money and mistakes. This applies at both levels.
points: Choose by skill level: a beginner needs a simple pattern with few darts and seams, and a pattern from an easy-sew range (a range of simple patterns) where one is offered.
Also choose by the design and purpose, by the buyer's preference, by the availability of suitable fabric, and by cost and the value it offers for the number of garments it can make.
Choose the size from body measurements: skirts and trousers are sized by hip measurement; dresses, shirts, coats and jackets are sized by bust or chest measurement. Waist is not the sizing measure.
The envelope gives the standard body measurements and the finished measurements of the garment, which show how much ease (room to move) the garment has.
The envelope lists the fabric quantity needed for each size and style, which stops you over- or under-buying, and whether the fabric should be plaid or diagonal-matched.
The envelope lists the notions needed, such as buttons, zips, interfacing, lining and trimmings, and the number of pattern pieces, so you can buy everything at once.
The envelope shows front and back views and suitable fabrics, which helps you avoid an unsuitable fabric, and it may include advice on the layout and construction order. It also gives the size range.
notes.tip: Factors in choosing a pattern, and the importance of one envelope item, are regular questions. When asked about one item, say why it matters, for example that fabric quantity prevents over- or under-buying.

notes.b: Pattern size is chosen from your measurements, so they must be accurate. Take them over light clothing, with the tape level and comfortably snug, not pulled tight, then compare them with the pattern's measurement chart to choose the size.
points: Bust or chest: measure around the fullest part of the bust or the chest.
Waist: measure around the natural waistline, with the tape held comfortably, not pulled tight.
Hips: measure around the widest part of the hips, keeping the tape level all the way round, because a tilted tape gives a false reading.
Nape to waist: measure from the most prominent bone at the base of the neck down to the waistline.
Inside leg: measure from the crotch down the inside of the leg to the required hemline. Shoulder is measured where needed.
notes.tip: For a question on measurements for a garment, name nape to waist, bust, waist and hip, and say where each is taken.

notes.h: Laying out and cutting the pattern
notes.b: Where and how the pieces are placed on the fabric decides how the finished garment hangs and looks. Accurate layout and cutting prevent twisted seams and wasted fabric.
points: Follow the pattern instructions and pin the pattern pieces to the fabric with the fabric folded as directed.
Place the straight grain of the pattern (the grain line marked on each piece) parallel to the selvedge (the finished edge of the fabric), so the garment hangs correctly.
Pattern pieces to be placed on a fold must sit exactly on the fold line, so the garment is symmetrical when opened out.
Take account of the nap, or direction of the pile, and of any pattern or print on the fabric, so that all pieces face the same way. Match checks and stripes at the seams.
Keep the fabric flat while pinning and cutting, and cut accurately around the pattern edges, then transfer the markings.
Diagram: pattern pieces on fabric showing the grain line parallel to the selvedge and a piece placed exactly on the fold.
notes.tip: If asked to list the stages of laying out a pattern, include following the instructions, pinning, grain parallel to the selvedge and fold pieces exactly on the fold.

notes.b: A plan of work puts the making in the right order so each step prepares the next. Evaluation follows once the garment is finished, as the last step of the design process.
points: Stage 1: lay out and cut the pattern pieces.
Stage 2: transfer markings and pin and tack (sew with temporary long stitches) the pieces together to check the fit.
Stage 3: machine sew and assemble the garment, joining darts and seams in the order the pattern gives, pressing as you go.
Stage 4: insert fastenings, attach facings and collars, add trimmings and complete the hems and edges.
Stage 5: press the seams and the finished garment, which removes creases and sets the shape, then evaluate the fit and finish and note any changes needed.
Pressing removes creases, defines darts, flattens seams and prevents puckering, so the garment looks professional.
Careful finishing means neatening seam allowances, clipping curves and trimming corners, so edges lie flat and do not fray.
notes.tip: Pressing during construction is a repeated question: say it improves the finished look, removes creases, defines darts, flattens seams and stops puckering. For a plan of work, give the stages in order.

notes.h: Modifying a commercial pattern (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A commercial pattern is made for a standard figure, so it is often changed to suit a particular person. Check any modification on the pattern before cutting.
points: A pattern is modified when the buyer's measurements differ from the size chosen, when the design needs a different length or width, or for a different style or preference.
Lengthen a pattern: cut through the alteration lines, spread the pieces, insert tissue paper and redraw the seam and fitting lines.
Shorten a pattern: fold along one of the alteration lines by half the amount to be removed, and redraw the seam and fitting lines.
Alteration lines are marked on the pattern, showing where the length can be changed.
Similar adjustments can change the width of the waist, hip, bust or sleeve by folding along the marked lines or cutting them.
Check the modification on the pattern, matching seams and keeping the grain line, before cutting the fabric.
notes.tip: For a question on modifying a pattern, describe lengthening or shortening and give suitable reasons, such as a non-standard figure, a different length or width, or personal preference.

notes.b: Elective 2 includes coursework in which you design and make a garment. These are the facts of the 2027 brief and how it is marked.
points: The coursework is worth 100 marks, or 10 per cent of the total marks: a design folder (25 marks) and a garment (75 marks).
The 2027 brief: design and sketch an outfit suitable for a young person to wear on holiday, expressing values, interests and personality; the outfit may be knitted, crocheted or machine stitched.
The candidate sets out the design specifications for the outfit, then makes and evaluates one garment from it.
The garment must include two of three processes: buttons and buttonholes; darts or shaping; a pocket.

Design folder marks: analysis and research 15, implementation 4, evaluation 6. The folder covers requirements, constraints, theme, sketches and justification, then the work sequence, then evaluation of the garment against the brief.
Garment marks: design aspects 15, skills and processes 50, finish 10.
The work must be the candidate's own, done under the teacher's supervision, with every source referenced, including any AI-generated material; the completion date is 6 April 2027.
notes.tip: Questions following up the coursework ask you to describe how to make a buttonhole, dart or patch pocket, or to evaluate a finished garment for fit, finish, comfort, function, appearance and changes.

notes.b: The garment must include two of three processes: buttons and buttonholes, darts or shaping, and a pocket. Each is made in a set order, and each is reinforced where it takes strain.
points: Buttonholes: mark the position and length (the button's diameter plus its thickness) on the right front for a woman's garment (left for men), at right angles to the edge for a horizontal hole, then reinforce with interfacing.
Buttonholes are worked by machine with a buttonhole foot or by hand with buttonhole stitch, and cut the opening last, without cutting the stitching.

Buttons: sew on to match the buttonholes, marked through the buttonhole position, with a thread shank (a short stem of thread) so the fastened layers lie flat; reinforce on fine or loosely woven fabric.

Darts (folded wedges that shape fabric to the body): transfer the dart markings from the pattern with tailor's chalk or tacking, fold right sides together matching the marks, stitch from the wide end to the point, and tie off or backstitch at the point.
Press bust and waist darts flat, then towards the centre or downward; the direction depends on the dart type and fabric.
Other shaping: gathers, pleats, tucks, princess seams and elastic also shape a garment to the body.
Patch pocket: mark the position, neaten and turn down the top edge as a facing, press under the seam allowances, and topstitch to the garment, reinforcing the top corners so they do not tear.
In-seam pocket: the pocket bag is stitched into a side seam so the opening is hidden.
Each process is interfaced or reinforced where it takes strain, and is pressed as it is made.
notes.tip: If asked to describe how to make a buttonhole, dart or patch pocket, give the steps in order and include the finishing detail, such as cutting the buttonhole open last or tying off the dart point.

keyTerms.definition: The set of requirements a garment must meet, including its purpose, the occasion and the budget.
A drawn design showing the garment's line, shape and features, with labels to explain them.
A full-scale tissue paper pattern for a garment, sold with an envelope that gives sizing and construction information.
The finished, non-fraying edge along each side of a woven fabric.
The line printed on a pattern piece that is placed parallel to the selvedge of the fabric.
The direction of the pile or surface pattern on a fabric, which must be kept the same on all pieces.
A marked line on a commercial pattern along which the pattern can be lengthened or shortened.
Long, temporary hand stitches used to hold pieces together before the garment is machine sewn.

questions.prompt: List the stages that should be followed when laying out and cutting a commercial pattern on fabric.
questions.model: Follow the pattern instructions; fold the fabric as directed. Place the straight grain of the pattern parallel to the selvedge. Place pieces that go on a fold exactly on the fold line. Consider the nap and any print on the fabric so all pieces face the same way. Pin the pieces flat, keep the fabric smooth, and cut accurately around the edges.

questions.prompt: Outline the design process a student would follow to make a garment for a specific brief, and explain how the design is evaluated once it is finished.
questions.model: Define and analyse the brief, identifying the purpose, occasion, budget and constraints of the garment. Investigate and research ideas from magazines, fabric samples and pattern books. Generate several possible ideas and present the best one as a labelled fashion sketch with a written description of its line, shape, colour, pattern, neckline, sleeves, fabric and accessories. Refine the design and select suitable fabric, testing its shrinkage, water repellence and crease recovery, and choose a commercial pattern that matches the wearer's measurements. Implement the design by laying out and cutting the pattern, pinning and tacking to check fit, machine sewing, inserting fastenings and finishing, and pressing. Evaluate the finished garment for fit, finish, comfort, function and appearance, against the original brief, and note any improvements for next time.
